angle: why rich people drive old cars, 15 rules from 3 angles: numbers, psychology, playbook
title: Why Rich People Drive Old Cars: 15 Money Rules From Real Millionaires

scenes.text: Hi, I'm Ryan Rover. Here's a question that tells you a lot about money. Why do so many genuinely rich people drive old, boring cars? You'd think the people who can most afford a brand new luxury car would be the ones buying them. But again and again, researchers find millionaires driving ten year old sedans, while people with far less money drive the shiny new SUVs. Today, we'll figure out why, through fifteen money rules from real millionaires.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: Here's the research that started it. In Stop Acting Rich, Thomas Stanley reported that the median price millionaires paid for their most recent vehicle was about thirty one thousand dollars, based on surveys in the late two thousands. Meanwhile, the average new car today sells for more than fifty thousand.

card.note: Different years, so treat as a rough contrast

scenes.short_hook: Why do so many millionaires drive old cars?

scenes.text: Those numbers come from different years, so they're not a perfect comparison. But the pattern is striking. Stanley found that many millionaires bought used cars, kept them for years, and chose reliable mainstream brands. He also found that a lot of the people driving luxury cars weren't millionaires at all. They were high earners spending their income on looking wealthy. That gap between looking rich and being rich is what this whole video is about.
scenes.query: Old reliable car parked in driveway
scenes.caption: LOOKING RICH VS BEING RICH

scenes.text: We'll go through fifteen rules from three angles. First, the numbers. The car math that millionaires understand and most people ignore. Second, the psychology. Why rich people don't need a car to feel successful. And third, the playbook. The rules they apply not just to cars, but to everything they buy. By the end, you'll see why an old car in a millionaire's driveway isn't a sign of being cheap. It's a sign of a strategy.
scenes.caption: THREE ANGLES

scenes.text: Let's begin with the numbers. Rule number one is the one that changes everything else.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: Our sources. Millionaire car data comes from Thomas Stanley's research. New car prices come from Kelley Blue Book, loan and payment data from Edmunds, and the full cost of owning a car from AAA's Your Driving Costs study. The average age of cars on American roads comes from S and P Global Mobility. Ideas on the psychology of money come from Morgan Housel's book The Psychology of Money and from research by psychologist Thomas Gilovich. Growth examples use a stated seven percent average yearly return, an illustration, not a promise. This is education, not financial advice.
scenes.caption: OUR SOURCES

scenes.text: Angle one. The numbers. Five rules about the math of cars, and why millionaires take that math so seriously.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: Rule number one. Let someone else pay for the biggest drop in value.

card.title: Let someone else pay the depreciation

scenes.caption: RULE 1
scenes.chapter: Rule 1. Let someone else pay the depreciation

scenes.text: A new car loses value fastest in its first few years. Sources like Carfax and Edmunds estimate that many new cars lose around twenty percent of their value in the first year, and roughly half or more within five years, depending on the model. That loss is called depreciation, and it's one of the biggest costs of owning a car. It never shows up on a bill, so most people never think about it. But it's real money leaving your pocket every single day.
scenes.query: New car driving off dealership lot
scenes.caption: -20% IN YEAR ONE
scenes.short_hook: Your new car loses this much in year one.

scenes.text: Millionaires who understand this often buy cars that are two or three years old. By then, the first owner has absorbed the steepest part of the drop. The car is often still reliable, may still have some warranty left, and costs thousands of dollars less. On a fifty thousand dollar car, letting someone else take the first year's hit could easily save ten thousand dollars or more. That's money that can be invested instead of evaporating in a driveway.
scenes.caption: LET SOMEONE ELSE PAY

scenes.text: Apply the rule. Before your next purchase, look up the price of the same model brand new and at two or three years old. Compare the difference with what you'd actually lose in features or reliability. For many reliable models, the slightly used version is the far better deal. Consider certified pre owned programs if you want extra peace of mind.
scenes.caption: NEW VS 3 YEARS OLD

scenes.text: Rule number two. Keep your car for a long, long time.

card.title: Keep it for ten years or more
card.sub: the cheapest car is the one you own

scenes.caption: RULE 2
scenes.chapter: Rule 2. Keep it for ten years or more

scenes.text: According to S and P Global Mobility, the average age of cars and light trucks on American roads has climbed to a record of over twelve and a half years. Modern cars, with good maintenance, can often last well over one hundred fifty thousand miles. Yet many people trade in every three to five years, starting a new cycle of depreciation and a new loan each time.
scenes.query: Old car with high mileage odometer
scenes.caption: 12.5 YEARS AVERAGE AGE

scenes.text: Every time you trade in a car, you lose money. Depreciation, sales tax, dealer fees, higher insurance on the newer car, and often a new loan with new interest. Keeping a car for ten years instead of five can cut your lifetime car costs dramatically. Many millionaires drive a car until repairs genuinely cost more than replacement. Not until they get bored.
scenes.caption: EVERY TRADE COSTS MONEY

scenes.text: Apply the rule. Set a goal to keep your current car at least five years past the final payment. Track repair costs in a notebook. Replace the car when repairs become frequent, expensive and unreliable, not when a new model comes out.
scenes.caption: DRIVE IT LONGER

scenes.text: Rule number three. Know the full cost of owning a car, not just the payment.
scenes.caption: RULE 3

scenes.text: AAA's Your Driving Costs study estimated that owning and operating a new car costs more than twelve thousand dollars a year on average when you add up depreciation, insurance, fuel, maintenance, financing, registration and taxes. That's over a thousand dollars a month. Most people only think about the monthly payment, which is just one piece of that total.
scenes.caption: $12,000+ A YEAR

scenes.text: Millionaires tend to think in total cost. A cheaper, reliable car doesn't just have a smaller payment. It usually has lower insurance, lower registration fees in many states, cheaper tires and parts, and less depreciation. The full cost difference between a modest car and a luxury car can be many thousands of dollars a year, every year.
scenes.caption: THE PAYMENT IS ONE PIECE

scenes.text: Apply the rule. Add up what your car really costs you in a year. Payment, insurance, fuel, maintenance, registration, parking and an estimate of depreciation. Divide by twelve. That's the real monthly price of your car. Use that number, not the payment, when you decide on your next one.
scenes.caption: THE REAL MONTHLY PRICE

scenes.text: Rule number four. Pay cash for cars when you can, and keep any loan short.

card.title: Pay cash, or keep the loan short

scenes.caption: RULE 4
scenes.chapter: Rule 4. Pay cash, or keep the loan short

scenes.text: Edmunds has reported that many new car loans now stretch to seventy two months or more, with average new car payments above seven hundred dollars a month. Long loans mean more interest and more time owing more than the car is worth. Many quiet millionaires either pay cash or use short loans they can pay off quickly.
scenes.caption: PAY CASH

scenes.text: There's a psychological benefit to cash too. When you have to hand over the full price, you feel it. That feeling makes you choose more carefully. A forty thousand dollar car feels very different as one payment from savings than as six hundred dollars a month. That's exactly why sellers push monthly payments.
scenes.caption: 72+ MONTH LOANS

scenes.text: Apply the rule. If you need a loan, aim for four years or less, and make a big down payment. Better yet, start a car fund now. When your current car loan ends, keep making the same payment into savings. By the time you need another car, you may be able to buy it outright.
scenes.caption: START A CAR FUND

scenes.text: Rule number five. Invest the difference.

card.title: Invest the difference
card.sub: the car that becomes a fortune

scenes.caption: RULE 5

scenes.text: Here's where the numbers get exciting. Say one person drives a modest used car, and another has a seven hundred dollar monthly payment on a new one. If the first person invests that seven hundred dollars every month instead, at a seven percent average yearly return, after twenty years it could grow to over three hundred sixty thousand dollars.
scenes.caption: INVEST THE DIFFERENCE

scenes.text: That's the secret behind the old car in the millionaire's driveway. It's not just about saving money on a car. It's about what the saved money becomes. Over a career, the difference between a car payment lifestyle and a paid off car lifestyle can easily reach hundreds of thousands of dollars, or more.
scenes.query: Modest car next to growing money
scenes.caption: WHAT THE OLD CAR BUYS

scenes.text: Apply the rule. Calculate the difference between what you spend on your car and what a reliable, modest car would cost. Even if it's only two hundred dollars a month, set up an automatic investment for that amount. Watch what it becomes.
scenes.caption: AUTOMATE IT

scenes.text: Here's the math on screen. Seven hundred dollars a month, invested for twenty years at a seven percent average yearly return, grows to roughly three hundred sixty five thousand dollars. You'd put in one hundred sixty eight thousand.
scenes.short_hook: What a car payment could become instead.

scenes.text: Let's compare two drivers over twenty years. Driver one buys a new fifty thousand dollar car every five years, trading in the old one each time. That's four new cars. Each time, they lose a big chunk to depreciation, pay sales tax again, and usually start a new loan with new interest. They're never without a car payment.
scenes.query: New car dealership row of cars
scenes.caption: DRIVER 1: NEW EVERY 5 YEARS
scenes.chapter: New every 5 years vs keep it for 10

scenes.text: Driver two buys a reliable three year old car for around thirty thousand dollars and keeps it ten years. Then they do it again. That's two cars in twenty years. They pay much less depreciation, much less sales tax, and spend many of those years with no payment at all. They also pay less for insurance and registration along the way.
scenes.caption: DRIVER 2: USED, KEEP 10 YEARS

scenes.text: The exact numbers depend on the cars, the loans and the market. But it's easy for the difference to reach well over one hundred thousand dollars in total costs over twenty years. Invested along the way, that difference could become several hundred thousand. Same need, getting from home to work. Completely different financial outcome.
scenes.caption: SAME NEED, DIFFERENT OUTCOME

scenes.text: That's angle one. Let someone else pay the depreciation, keep it ten years, know the full cost, pay cash or keep loans short, and invest the difference. Now angle two. The psychology. Because the numbers are easy. The hard part is not caring what other people think.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: For many people, a car isn't just transportation. It's a statement. It says who you are, how successful you are, what kind of person you want to be seen as. Car companies spend enormous amounts on advertising that connects their cars with status, freedom and identity. Millionaires who drive old cars have learned to separate those feelings from the purchase.
scenes.caption: A CAR AS A STATEMENT

scenes.text: Rule number six. Your car is a tool, not your identity.

card.title: A car is transportation, not identity
card.sub: who you are isn't parked outside

scenes.caption: RULE 6
scenes.chapter: Rule 6. A car is transportation, not identity

scenes.text: Stanley found that many millionaires simply didn't care much about cars. They saw a car as a tool to get from one place to another, safely and reliably. Many found satisfaction elsewhere, in their families, their businesses, their communities and their financial independence. Their identity wasn't parked in the driveway.
scenes.caption: A TOOL

scenes.text: When your car is part of your identity, every few years you feel pressure to upgrade it, because the old one no longer matches who you think you are. When your car is just a tool, you replace it when it stops working. That one shift in thinking can save a fortune over a lifetime.
scenes.caption: IDENTITY LIVES ELSEWHERE

scenes.text: Apply the rule. Ask yourself honestly what you want your car to say about you. Then ask whether there's a cheaper way to be that person. Usually, the things we want to be known for, like being successful, reliable or interesting, have nothing to do with what we drive.
scenes.caption: WHAT DO YOU WANT IT TO SAY?

scenes.text: Rule number seven. Nobody is watching you as closely as you think.

card.title: Nobody is watching as much as you think

scenes.caption: RULE 7
scenes.chapter: Rule 7. Nobody is watching as much as you think

scenes.text: Psychologist Thomas Gilovich and his colleagues studied something called the spotlight effect. In one famous experiment, students wore an embarrassing T shirt into a room, and they greatly overestimated how many people noticed it. We all tend to believe others are paying much more attention to us than they really are.
scenes.caption: THE SPOTLIGHT EFFECT
scenes.short_hook: Nobody is watching you as much as you think.

scenes.text: That applies to cars too. You might think people judge you for your old sedan. In reality, most people are too busy thinking about themselves to notice. Millionaires who drive old cars seem to understand this intuitively. They don't spend money performing for an audience that isn't really there.
scenes.caption: EVERYONE IS BUSY WITH THEMSELVES

scenes.text: Apply the rule. Next time you feel embarrassed about your car, ask yourself when you last noticed what a coworker or neighbor drove, and whether you thought less of them for it. Probably never. They're not thinking about yours either.
scenes.caption: NOBODY NOTICES

scenes.text: Rule number eight. Real wealth is invisible.

card.title: Wealth is what you don't see
card.sub: the man in the car paradox

scenes.caption: RULE 8
scenes.chapter: Rule 8. Wealth is what you don't see

scenes.text: In The Psychology of Money, Morgan Housel describes what he calls the man in the car paradox. When you see someone driving a nice car, you rarely think, wow, that driver is cool. You think, wow, if I had that car, people would think I'm cool. The irony is that people who buy expensive things to earn admiration often don't get it, because observers are imagining themselves in the car.
scenes.caption: THE MAN IN THE CAR PARADOX
scenes.short_hook: Nobody admires you for your car. Here's why.

scenes.text: Housel also points out that wealth is what you don't see. It's the cars not bought, the upgrades not made, the money left invested. A big house or a fancy car might mean someone is rich, or it might mean they're deeply in debt. You can't tell from the outside. Real wealth is the money still in the account.
scenes.caption: WEALTH IS INVISIBLE

scenes.text: Apply the rule. Next time you're tempted to buy something to impress, remember the paradox. People won't admire you. They'll imagine themselves with it. If you want respect, kindness and generosity work far better, and cost much less.
scenes.caption: RESPECT COSTS LESS

scenes.text: Rule number nine. Be willing to wait.
scenes.caption: RULE 9

scenes.text: In the famous Stanford marshmallow studies, children who could wait for a second treat instead of eating one right away were followed into adulthood. Later research has questioned how much those results really predict, and found that family background matters a lot. But the basic idea still resonates with how many millionaires behave. They're willing to wait.
scenes.caption: THE MARSHMALLOW TEST

scenes.text: Driving an old car now so you can have financial freedom later is a form of delayed gratification. The new car feels good immediately. The investments feel good much later. People who build wealth have usually learned to enjoy the waiting, or at least to see it as a fair trade.
scenes.caption: WILLING TO WAIT

scenes.text: Apply the rule. When you want a big purchase, set a waiting period. Thirty days for anything over a few hundred dollars, six months for a car. Use the time to save for it in cash. If you still want it after the wait, buy it with no regrets.
scenes.caption: SAVE WHILE YOU WAIT

scenes.text: Let's take a quick break. If you're enjoying these rules, subscribe to Ryan Rover Money. It's free and it helps the channel grow, so we can keep making long, honest videos about money. Now, rule number ten, which explains why the new car feeling never lasts.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: Rule number ten. Get off the hedonic treadmill.
scenes.caption: RULE 10

scenes.text: Psychologists use the term hedonic adaptation, often called the hedonic treadmill, to describe how we quickly get used to new things. The thrill of a new car fades within months. It becomes just your car. Then you start wanting the next upgrade to feel that thrill again, and the cycle repeats.
scenes.caption: THE HEDONIC TREADMILL

scenes.text: People who understand this stop chasing the thrill through things. Instead, they find longer lasting satisfaction in experiences, relationships, health and the security of having money saved. Research on happiness has often suggested that experiences and time with people we love bring more lasting joy than possessions.
scenes.caption: EXPERIENCES LAST LONGER

scenes.text: Apply the rule. Think about the last big purchase that excited you. How long did the excitement last? Use that answer the next time you're tempted. And consider spending that money on an experience you'll remember instead.
scenes.caption: WHAT DO YOU REMEMBER?

scenes.text: There's one more psychological reason rich people often drive old cars. Once you have real financial security, you need less external proof of success. You know you're doing well, because your accounts tell you so. People who don't yet have that security often feel more pressure to show success through things.
scenes.caption: SECURITY BEATS STATUS
scenes.chapter: Why rich people care less about status

scenes.text: This creates a strange loop. The people who most need to save are often the ones who feel the most pressure to spend on status. And the people who've already saved feel the least pressure. Breaking that loop early, by caring less about what others see, is one of the most powerful money moves anyone can make.
scenes.caption: BREAK THE LOOP

scenes.text: Many millionaires describe a quiet satisfaction in knowing that they could buy the luxury car, and choosing not to. That feeling of freedom, of having options, is often worth more to them than the car itself. Financial independence is the ultimate status symbol, and it's one nobody else can see.
scenes.caption: THE ULTIMATE STATUS SYMBOL

scenes.text: That's angle two. A car is a tool, nobody's watching, wealth is invisible, be willing to wait, and get off the treadmill. Now angle three, the playbook. Five rules millionaires apply not just to cars, but to everything.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: The old car isn't really about cars. It's a symptom of a whole way of handling money. The same rules show up in how millionaires buy houses, clothes, electronics and almost everything else. Here are the five that matter most.
scenes.caption: BEYOND CARS

scenes.text: Rule number eleven. Take care of what you already own.

card.title: Maintenance beats replacement
card.sub: take care of what you own

scenes.caption: RULE 11

scenes.text: Regular oil changes, tire rotations and following the maintenance schedule can help a car last far longer. The same applies to homes, appliances and clothes. Small maintenance costs today often prevent big replacement costs tomorrow. Many millionaires are meticulous about maintenance for exactly this reason.
scenes.caption: MAINTENANCE

scenes.text: Skipping maintenance is a false saving. A neglected car can need expensive repairs years earlier than a maintained one. A neglected roof can damage the whole house. Taking care of what you own is one of the most reliable ways to spend less over time.
scenes.caption: SMALL COSTS PREVENT BIG ONES

scenes.text: Apply the rule. Find your car's maintenance schedule in the owner's manual and follow it. Do the same for your home, with a simple yearly checklist. Fix small problems early, before they turn into big ones.
scenes.caption: FOLLOW THE SCHEDULE

scenes.text: Rule number twelve. Don't borrow for things that lose value.

card.title: Borrow only for things that grow

scenes.caption: RULE 12
scenes.chapter: Rule 12. Borrow only for things that grow

scenes.text: Many financially careful people follow a simple principle. Borrowing might make sense for things that can grow in value or income, like a reasonable mortgage, an education with a clear payoff, or a business. But borrowing for things that lose value, like cars, vacations and electronics, makes you poorer twice. You pay interest on something that's shrinking.
scenes.caption: BORROW FOR GROWTH

scenes.text: Car loans are the most common example. You pay interest every month on an asset that's losing value every month. That's why so many millionaires prefer to pay cash for cars, or at least keep loans short, even when they could easily afford the payments.
scenes.caption: INTEREST ON A SHRINKING ASSET

scenes.text: Apply the rule. Look at every loan you have. Is it for something that grows, or something that shrinks? Prioritize paying off the loans on shrinking things first, especially if they have high interest rates.
scenes.caption: PAY OFF THE SHRINKERS

scenes.text: Rule number thirteen. Insure against disasters, not inconveniences.
scenes.caption: RULE 13

scenes.text: Older cars often don't need the same insurance as new ones. Once a car's value drops, some owners decide that collision coverage costs more than it's worth, especially if they have the savings to replace the car. Raising deductibles, when you have an emergency fund, can also lower premiums.
scenes.caption: INSURE SMART

scenes.text: The bigger principle is that wealthy people insure against losses they couldn't handle, like liability in a serious accident, while self insuring small losses. That's why liability coverage stays important even on an old car. A serious accident can lead to costs far bigger than the car itself.
scenes.caption: LIABILITY MATTERS

scenes.text: Apply the rule. Check your car insurance this year. Compare what you pay for collision coverage with what the car is actually worth. Make sure your liability limits are high enough. And shop around for quotes at least once a year.
scenes.caption: SHOP EVERY YEAR

scenes.text: Rule number fourteen. Make good decisions automatic.
scenes.caption: RULE 14

scenes.text: Millionaires who drive old cars aren't superhuman. Many have simply set up systems so the right choices happen without effort. Automatic transfers to retirement accounts, automatic payments into a car fund, automatic bill payments so late fees never happen.
scenes.caption: AUTOMATE IT

scenes.text: Automation protects you from your own worst moments. If money is moved to investments on payday, there's less sitting in checking to be tempted by a new car ad. The default becomes saving, and spending becomes the active choice.
scenes.caption: SAVING BY DEFAULT

scenes.text: Apply the rule. This week, set up three automatic transfers. One to retirement, one to an emergency fund, and one to a car fund. Start small. You can always increase them later.
scenes.caption: THREE TRANSFERS

scenes.text: And rule number fifteen. Spend lavishly on what you love, and cut ruthlessly on what you don't.

card.title: Spend big on what you love
card.sub: and cut ruthlessly on the rest

scenes.caption: RULE 15
scenes.chapter: Rule 15. Spend big on what you love

scenes.text: Personal finance author Ramit Sethi calls this conscious spending. The idea is that being good with money doesn't mean cutting everything. It means deciding what you truly value, spending freely on that, and cutting costs mercilessly on things you don't care about.
scenes.caption: SPEND ON WHAT YOU LOVE

scenes.text: That's exactly why so many millionaires drive old cars. They don't care about cars, so they spend as little as possible on them. But many spend generously on things they value, like travel, their kids' education, charity or a hobby. Their spending isn't small. It's focused. And because it's focused, it actually makes them happier than spending a little bit on everything ever could.
scenes.caption: FOCUSED, NOT SMALL

scenes.text: Apply the rule. Write down three things you truly love spending money on. Then write down three things you spend on but don't really care about. Cut the second list, and feel free to enjoy the first. That's not being cheap. It's being intentional.
scenes.caption: LOVE IT OR CUT IT

scenes.text: Now let's make this practical. Here's how to buy your next car the way a quiet millionaire would, step by step.
scenes.caption: RYAN
scenes.chapter: How to buy a car the millionaire way

scenes.text: Step one. Decide your budget before you shop, based on the full cost of ownership, not the payment. A rule of thumb many personal finance writers use is to keep your total vehicle costs, including payment, insurance and fuel, to a modest share of your take home pay, often suggested as around ten to fifteen percent. Write the number down before you ever set foot on a lot, because dealerships are designed to make you forget it.
scenes.caption: STEP 1: SET THE BUDGET

scenes.text: Step two. Pick models known for reliability. Look at reliability ratings from sources like Consumer Reports, and check crash safety ratings from the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety. Reliable mainstream models tend to hold their value reasonably well and cost less to repair. A boring car with a great reliability record is often the smartest purchase on the lot.
scenes.caption: STEP 2: CHOOSE RELIABLE

scenes.text: Step three. Check the history and get an inspection. Run a vehicle history report to check for accidents, flood damage and title problems. Then pay an independent mechanic to inspect the car before you buy. It usually costs a modest fee and can save you from a very expensive mistake. Sellers who refuse an inspection are telling you something.
scenes.caption: STEP 3: INSPECT IT

scenes.text: Step four. Arrange financing before you shop, if you need it. Credit unions and banks often offer better rates than dealer financing. With a pre approval in hand, you can negotiate on the total price, not the monthly payment. Step five. Negotiate the out the door price, which includes taxes and fees. And be ready to walk away. There are always more cars.
scenes.caption: STEPS 4 AND 5: FINANCE AND NEGOTIATE

scenes.text: Step six. Say no to the extras in the finance office. Extended warranties, paint protection, fabric protection, and other add ons are often heavily marked up. If you want a warranty, you can research options separately and take your time. And step seven. Once you drive home, start your car fund immediately, so the next car is paid for before you need it.
scenes.caption: STEPS 6 AND 7: NO EXTRAS, START THE FUND

scenes.text: In your twenties, the car rule matters most, because every dollar not spent on a car can compound for forty years. A reliable used car, paid in cash or with a short loan, is one of the best financial decisions a young person can make. Many people who become millionaires look back on driving a cheap car in their twenties as a turning point.
scenes.caption: IN YOUR 20s
scenes.chapter: Your car plan at every stage

scenes.text: In your thirties and forties, family needs often grow. Safety and space matter more. That's fine. The same rules apply. Buy a few years old, choose reliability, keep it long, and avoid long loans. A minivan you keep for twelve years can be a fantastic financial decision. Two car households can also stagger purchases so they're never replacing both cars at once.
scenes.caption: IN YOUR 30s AND 40s

scenes.text: In your fifties and beyond, many people finally have the financial room to buy a nicer car. If your retirement is on track, a car you truly enjoy might be part of your conscious spending. Just remember that every car is still a depreciating asset, and that money spent on cars close to retirement has fewer years to recover.
scenes.query: Older couple with car on road trip
scenes.caption: IN YOUR 50s AND BEYOND

scenes.text: Let's look at the car mistakes that cost people the most. Mistake one. Rolling negative equity into a new loan. If you owe more than your car is worth and trade it in, the dealer may add the leftover balance to your new loan. You start the new car already underwater, paying interest on a car you no longer own.
scenes.caption: MISTAKE 1: ROLLING NEGATIVE EQUITY
scenes.chapter: The five most expensive car mistakes

scenes.text: Mistake two. Shopping by monthly payment. When the only question is what payment you can handle, a seller can stretch the loan, add extras and raise the price, all while keeping the payment the same. Mistake three. Leasing forever. Leasing can make sense in some situations, but leasing one car after another means you always have a payment and never own anything.
scenes.caption: MISTAKES 2 AND 3

scenes.text: Mistake four. Buying more car than your life needs. A large truck or SUV for a solo commute costs more in fuel, insurance and depreciation. Buy for the life you actually live, not the one in the commercial. And mistake five. Skipping maintenance to save money, which often turns a cheap fix into an expensive repair, and shortens the life of the car.
scenes.caption: MISTAKES 4 AND 5

scenes.text: Here's the bigger lesson. The old car rule works for almost everything you buy. Houses. Buy what you need, take care of it, and stay long enough to avoid the costs of moving again and again. Phones. Keep them until they genuinely stop working well. Clothes. Buy quality where it matters, wear it for years, and skip the trends.
scenes.caption: THE RULE FOR EVERYTHING
scenes.chapter: The old car rule for everything else

scenes.text: The pattern is always the same. Buy something good enough, often slightly used. Take care of it. Keep it much longer than most people do. And invest the money you didn't spend on upgrades. Do that across your whole life, and the results can be enormous, because you're not just saving on one car. You're saving on hundreds of purchases over decades.
scenes.caption: GOOD ENOUGH, KEPT LONG

scenes.text: That's really why rich people drive old cars. It's not one decision. It's a philosophy that shows up everywhere in their lives. The car is just the most visible example, because it's sitting right there in the driveway for everyone to see.
scenes.caption: THE VISIBLE EXAMPLE

scenes.text: Let me give you a few real examples of wealthy people who are famous for modest cars.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: Warren Buffett, one of the richest people in the world, has been known for years for driving ordinary cars and keeping them a long time. He has joked in interviews that he only drives a few thousand miles a year, so he doesn't need a new car very often. For a man worth well over one hundred billion dollars, the car simply isn't important.
scenes.caption: WARREN BUFFETT

scenes.text: And then there are the quiet millionaires you'll never hear about. The retired teacher with a paid off house and a twelve year old Camry. The plumber who owns his business and drives a work truck with two hundred thousand miles on it. The engineer who bought a three year old minivan and drove it until her kids went to college. Stanley's research is full of people like them.
scenes.caption: THE QUIET MILLIONAIRES

scenes.text: None of them are depriving themselves. They still enjoy road trips, family vacations and nice dinners. They just decided, long ago, that the car wasn't where they wanted their money to go. Over decades, that one decision freed up a fortune. And that fortune bought them something no car can buy, which is freedom.
scenes.caption: FREEDOM

scenes.text: Question one. Aren't old cars unsafe? Safety has improved a lot over the years, so it's worth checking crash test ratings from the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety and the government's NHTSA before you buy. But many cars that are a few years old have excellent safety features. Driving a modest car doesn't mean driving an unsafe one.
scenes.caption: ARE OLD CARS SAFE?

scenes.text: Question two. Don't repairs on an old car cost more than a payment? Sometimes, but often not. Even a major repair costing a couple thousand dollars is usually far less than a year of new car payments. The key is to budget for repairs in advance with a car fund, so they don't become emergencies.
scenes.caption: REPAIRS VS PAYMENTS

scenes.text: Question three. What about electric cars? Many electric cars cost less to fuel and maintain, which can help the total cost. The same rules still apply. Consider buying used, check the battery warranty and condition, keep it a long time, and calculate the full cost of ownership.
scenes.caption: WHAT ABOUT EVs?

scenes.text: Question four. Can I ever buy my dream car? Absolutely. If you love cars, it can be part of your conscious spending. The millionaire way is to buy it after you've built a strong financial base, pay cash or keep the loan short, and cut costs elsewhere to make room for it.
scenes.caption: THE DREAM CAR

scenes.text: Question five. What if I need a reliable car for work? Then reliability is exactly what you should pay for. Choose models with strong reliability ratings, have a trusted mechanic inspect any used car before buying, and keep an emergency fund so a breakdown doesn't threaten your job.
scenes.caption: RELIABILITY FOR WORK

scenes.text: Question six. Should I lease or buy? For most people who want to minimize lifetime car costs, buying a reliable car and keeping it for many years tends to be cheaper than leasing one car after another. Leasing can make sense for some business owners or people who drive very few miles and want a new car every few years, but it means a permanent payment. Read every lease term carefully, especially mileage limits and wear charges.
scenes.caption: LEASE OR BUY?

scenes.text: Question seven. How do I start a car fund if I still have a car loan? Start small now, even fifty dollars a month, while you finish the loan. When the loan is paid off, add the full old payment to the fund. In a few years, you'll have enough to buy your next car in cash, and you'll never need a car loan again. That one cycle change can save you thousands in interest over your lifetime.
scenes.caption: STARTING A CAR FUND

scenes.text: Quick recap. Angle one, the numbers. Let someone else pay the depreciation, keep it ten years or more, know the full cost, pay cash or keep loans short, and invest the difference.
scenes.caption: THE NUMBERS: 1 TO 5

scenes.text: Angle two, the psychology. A car is transportation, not identity. Nobody is watching as much as you think. Wealth is what you don't see. Delay gratification. And escape the hedonic treadmill.
scenes.caption: THE PSYCHOLOGY: 6 TO 10

scenes.text: Angle three, the playbook. Maintenance beats replacement, borrow only for things that grow, insure smart, automate the good choices, and spend big on what you love while cutting ruthlessly on the rest.
scenes.caption: THE PLAYBOOK: 11 TO 15

scenes.text: Here's the big idea one more time. A car is one of the largest purchases most people make, over and over, for their entire lives. Getting that one decision right, again and again, can be worth more than almost any investment tip you'll ever hear. Buy reliable, buy slightly used, keep it long, and invest the difference. So next time you see an old car in a nice neighborhood, don't assume the owner is struggling. They might be the richest person on the street. If you want the full plan for building that kind of quiet wealth, it's in my playbook, linked in the description. Tell me in the comments how old your car is. I'm Ryan Rover. See you in the next one.
scenes.caption: RYAN
